title: Catalog criteria & buyer personas - quick draft
body:
Purpose:
Quick working draft to align on how we position the model catalog (open models + Redwood’s verified profiles) for three core buyer segments and to surface competitive gaps we should call out. This is intentionally rough — meant for internal review and to feed into the landing page / sales one-pager iteration.

Context & problem statement:
- Buyers increasingly expect access to open models but they don’t trust "open" alone: they need measurable, comparable signals (latency, evals, cost) and an ops story for serving at scale.
- 'Verified profile' should be our structured answer: a short, consistent package of artifacts that reduce discovery friction and procurement risk.
- We need messaging that ties technical signals to buyer outcomes (time-to-ship, predictable unit cost, regulatory auditability).

What a Verified Profile should include (candidate list):
- Model name + common family aliases (for discovery)
- Reference workloads (short bulleted examples matched to common GTM use cases)
- Latency percentiles at X and Y sequence lengths on Redwood S/T/D (p50/p95/p99)
- Token cost estimates (hosted and dedicated) with assumptions spelled out
- Eval snapshot: curated evals (safety, hallucination, instruction-following) + a short interpretation of failure modes
- Compatibility matrix: supported endpoints/features (streaming, functions, embeddings, kv-cache)
- Size / quantization profiles tested (FP16, Q4, Q8, any specialized kernels)
- Rollout suggestions & fallback compatibility (e.g., suggested smaller family for warm fallback)
- Ops notes: memory footprint, warmup characteristics, batching sensitivity
- Link to canonical reproducible benchmark (not just proprietary numbers)

Competitive signals and how we differentiate (notes):
- Generic LLM APIs (some competitors): emphasize that they provide model access but rarely include reproducible serving profiles or rollout guidance tuned for production economics.
- Self-host runtimes / infra vendors: they promote low-level control; our angle is 'we do the heavy engineering and provide standardized profiles + verified runtime numbers so teams can buy time, not just software'.
- Managed-model vendors with curated catalogs: call out where they give opaque "benchmarks" vs our emphasis on percentile latency + quantization artifacts + evals tied to sample prompts.

Buyer personas + positioning hooks:
1) Startup PM / Founder building a user-facing feature
   - Decision drivers: speed to prototype, cost predictability, minimal ops burden
   - Messaging: "Pick a model with a verified profile that shows real-world latency and cost for your workload. Ship faster — we handle warmup/caching knobs so you don't have to."
   - Demo idea: 2-click model swap in a simple chat app showing latency/throughput differences and cost-estimates.

2) Platform / Infra Engineer at mid-market / enterprise
   - Decision drivers: operational reliability, compatibility with infra, rollout/fallback strategies, observability
   - Messaging: "Profiles include p95/p99 latency on our runtime and explicit fallback compatibility matrices so you can safely A/B and roll back without surprises."
   - Proof point to show: traced request flow, KV-cache behavior, burst scaling policy that matched a customer incident.

3) Security/Compliance / Procurement
   - Decision drivers: reproducible audits, data isolation, clear SLAs and evidence of model behavior (safety evals), licensing clarity
   - Messaging: "Verified profiles attach signed eval snapshots, model licensing notes, and a reproducible benchmark harness to support audits."
   - Extra ask: a one-page audit artifact template we can generate per-profile.

Concrete messaging frames (short lines for web / deck):
- Outcome frame: "Choose with confidence: production-ready model profiles for predictable latency, cost and safety."
- Economics frame: "Compare apples-to-apples: token cost + runtime-percentiles so finance can forecast unit economics."
- Ops frame: "Verified for serving: rollout guidance, fallback options, and observable metrics shipped with every profile."

Experiments to run (MVP backlog):
- A: Create 12 canonical verified profiles for top 3 model families users ask about. Publish a single-page "compare" view that shows p50/p95/p99, cost estimate, and 2-line eval summary.
- B: Sales enablement one-pager per persona: quick checklist + sample audit artifact.
- C: Landing page A/B where one variant highlights "verified profiles (technical signals)" and the other highlights "editor's picks" (curation only). Measure signups and request-for-demo conversion.

Risks / tradeoffs:
- Too many signals = cognitive load. Need a canonical subset for the main UI with expandable details.
- Benchmarks can be gamed. Must publish methodology and make raw harnesses available (or reproducible scripts) to build trust.
- Data freshness: model behaviors change after quantization/patches; need a refresh cadence (suggest 30/90 days depending on model churn).

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Minimum viable field-set for verified profile in the product UI? (propose: latency p95, token cost, one safety eval sentence, compatibility matrix)
- How do we surface quantization tradeoffs (Q4 vs Q8) without confusing non-engineering buyers?
- Who on eng side owns the canonical reproducible harness and public artifacts? (cc: @marcus for infra/benchmarks)
- What license/attribution checks are required for archiving model artifacts/links in the profile?

Next steps (owner / timeline):
- Finalize canonical verified profile schema: owner Marcus Patel, due 2024-11-01.
- Build 12 profile MVP set: product+research pair (Elena Ruiz + Jae Kim), due 2024-11-15.
- Landing page A/B + sales one-pagers: go-to-market owner Ariana Chen, initial experiment by 2024-12-01.

Action items (short):
action_items: Marcus: draft canonical profile schema (include required fields and examples) - due 2024-11-01
Elena + Jae: build 12 MVP verified profiles and reproducible harness links - due 2024-11-15
Ariana: write two landing copy variants and coordinate A/B test - due 2024-11-30
Engineering: confirm ownership of benchmark harness and public artifact storage - sync meeting week of 2024-10-15
competitors: Large LLM API providers (opaque benchmarks, broad model access; gap: reproducible runtime profiles)
Self-host runtimes / infra vendors (control focus; gap: curated, buyer-facing profiles and economics)
Managed model catalogs (curation heavy; gap: reproducible artifacts + percentile latencies + rollout guidance)
buyer_personas: Startup PM - cares about speed to market, low ops overhead, cost predictability
Platform Engineer - cares about p95/p99 latency, compatibility, safe rollouts
Security/Compliance - cares about auditability, eval artifacts, clear licensing
key_messages: Production-ready signals: standardized latency and cost numbers you can rely on
Operational playbooks shipped with models: rollout + fallback + quantization guidance
Audit-ready artifacts: signed eval snapshots and reproducible benchmark harnesses
open_questions: What is the MVP field-set for a profile in the UI?
How often should profiles be re-benchmarked? 30/60/90 days?
What is the public vs internal artifact policy for raw benchmark outputs?
